cognate: no cognate verb between the two anchors: OHG hōren (*h₂ḱh₂ows-) vs Skt śru (*ḱlew-); but Greek ἀκούω is the exact cognate of hōren and Il. 2.486 joins it with κλέος (= the śru root), and Il. 24.543 uses ἀκούομεν exactly as śuśruma, for what tradition says of a past ruler
drift_or_renewal: verb renewed: *ḱlew- 'hear' (Skt śuśruma) replaced by *h₂ḱh₂ows- (OHG hôrtih, Gk ἀκούομεν, Germanic also *fregnan in Wessobrunn/OE gefrægn)
shared_syntax: 1st-person perfect/preterite of 'hear' (+ optional 'tell'/iti) introducing a report taken from tradition, not from sight: 'I heard X tell that ...' / 'thus we have heard'
context: poet or narrator cites oral tradition as the source of knowledge about the distant past or end of the world: Muspilli 'Daz hôrtih rahhôn dia uueroltrehtuuison' (the world-law-wise) introducing Elias vs Antichrist; MBh 'tān pañca samrājaḥ iti śuśrumaḥ' about the five ancient universal kings; Il. 2.486 'we only hear the fame, we know nothing'. Muspilli is Christian 9th-c. and the formula is also Hildebrandslied's opening, so it is native Germanic poetic diction rather than a Latin calque
phrase: 'I/we have heard (it told)' as the source-formula of traditional poetry
